title: Extremists, Swadeshi and Revolutionaries

cards.b: After 1900 a new generation wanted boycott, not begging. The partition of Bengal in 1905 gave them a cause.

Causes: Moderates’ failure, Curzon’s policies (Calcutta Corporation Act 1899, Official Secrets Act 1904, University Act 1904, partition of Bengal 1905), economic distress (famines, plague), Japan’s victory over Russia in 1905, and the work of Vivekananda and Dayanand. Leaders: Lal-Bal-Pal (Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal) and Aurobindo Ghose.

Announced July 1905 by Curzon, effective 16 October 1905. East Bengal and Assam (Muslim-majority) separated from West Bengal. The stated reason was administrative efficiency. The real aim was to divide the Hindu and Muslim population and weaken Bengal. 16 October was observed as a day of mourning and rakhi bandhan (Tagore’s songs, e.g. “Amar Sonar Bangla”). The partition was annulled in 1911 at the Delhi Durbar, and the capital moved to Delhi.

Declared on 7 August 1905 at the Calcutta Town Hall. Methods: boycott of foreign goods, national education (National Council of Education, 1906; Bengal National College, Aurobindo as principal), samitis (Swadesh Bandhab Samiti, Ashwini Kumar Dutt), swadeshi industry (Bengal Chemicals, Tata Steel, 1907), and the use of melas and festivals (Ganapati, Shivaji). The four aims adopted at the 1906 Calcutta Congress (Naoroji) were Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education.

At Surat (December 1907) the Congress broke into Moderates and Extremists. The issue: the presidency (Lajpat Rai vs Rash Behari Ghosh) and the resolutions on boycott and swadeshi. The government then repressed the Extremists: Tilak was jailed for six years in Mandalay (1908), Aurobindo and Lajpat Rai were arrested or exiled. The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 gave separate electorates to Muslims. The two wings reunited at Lucknow, 1916.

• Bengal: Anushilan Samiti, Jugantar; Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki (1908 Muzaffarpur).
  • Maharashtra: Chapekar brothers (1897, Rand); Savarkar’s Abhinav Bharat.
  • Abroad: India House (Shyamji Krishnavarma, London); Madan Lal Dhingra (1909); Ghadar Party (1913, San Francisco; Lala Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna); Komagata Maru (1914).
The Alipore Bomb case (1908) involved Aurobindo.

After Chauri Chaura the youth turned to the gun. HRA (1924, Sachindranath Sanyal) → Kakori (1925; Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan). HSRA (1928; Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekhar Azad). Saunders’ killing (1928), Assembly bomb (1929), Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev hanged 23 March 1931. Surya Sen’s Chittagong armoury raid (1930). Subhas Bose’s INA is the last wave.

Gandhi opposed terrorism but admired its courage. Bipan Chandra says revolutionaries gave fearlessness and a symbol but lacked mass support. Their ideas moved towards socialism (HSRA, Bhagat Singh’s “Why I am an atheist”, 1930). Critics point to the narrow and elitist social base.

Swadeshi lives on in “Make in India” and “Atmanirbhar Bharat”. Dates such as 23 March (Shaheed Diwas) and the memorial at Hussainiwala keep memory alive. The Bengal partition shaped regional identity (1947, 1971).

• “Differences between the Moderates and Extremists.” Compare goal, methods, social base, leaders.
  • “Significance of the Swadeshi movement.”
